summary: The book closes with procedures for vows and dedications involving persons, animals, houses, fields, firstborn animals, permanently devoted things, and tithes. Priestly valuations, redemption payments, added fifths, and Jubilee timing prevent a dedication from depending only on a private promise or improvised price.
whyItMatters: The final chapter gives vows and dedications definite payment, property, and redemption consequences. It distinguishes arrangements that can be bought back from things permanently devoted, including a separate and severe rule about a person devoted to destruction.

context.author: Leviticus presents Yahweh giving these vow rules to Moses; the finished book does not name its narrator, and its composition history remains debated.
context.audience: Israelites making vows or dedications and priests responsible for valuation, redemption, and protected holy property.
context.date: The rules are narrated at Mount Sinai and assume the Jubilee system in the land; the date of the book's received literary form is debated.
context.setting: Israelite households, herds, houses, fields, sanctuary valuations, and tithes viewed through their dedication to Yahweh.
context.literaryForm: A concluding legal appendix of valuation and redemption cases, followed by a Sinai colophon.

outline.heading: Valuations for persons named in vows
outline.note: Fixed silver amounts vary by age and sex, with a priest-adjusted amount for someone unable to pay.

outline.heading: Dedicated animals and houses
outline.note: Eligible animals cannot simply be exchanged, while unclean animals and houses may be redeemed with an added fifth.

outline.heading: Fields valued by seed and Jubilee
outline.note: Possessed and purchased fields receive different redemption and return rules based on years remaining.

outline.heading: Firstborn animals already belonging to Yahweh
outline.note: A firstborn eligible animal cannot be newly dedicated, while an unclean firstborn may be redeemed or sold.

outline.heading: Permanently devoted things and a difficult death rule
outline.note: Irredeemable devoted property leads into an unexplained and contested statement about a person devoted to destruction.

outline.heading: Tithes of land and livestock
outline.note: A tenth is holy, with an added fifth for redeemed produce and no selective exchange of herd animals.

outline.heading: The Sinai commandments concluded
outline.note: The book ends by locating the commandments with Yahweh, Moses, Israel, and Mount Sinai.

keyVerses.text: But if he is poorer than your valuation, then he shall be set before the priest, and the priest shall assign a value to him. The priest shall assign a value according to his ability to pay.
keyVerses.why: A person unable to meet the standard valuation receives an amount based on ability to pay.

keyVerses.text: In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought, even to him to whom the possession of the land belongs.
keyVerses.why: A dedicated purchased field still returns to its ancestral owner at Jubilee.

keyVerses.text: “‘No one devoted to destruction, who shall be devoted from among men, shall be ransomed. He shall surely be put to death.
keyVerses.why: The text distinguishes a person devoted to destruction as irredeemable and subject to death.

themes: what is already or permanently holy

questions.question: What is being valued when a person is named in a vow?
questions.answer: Verses 2–8 regulate the monetary obligation associated with consecrating a person in a vow. The stated amounts are silver payments, and the priest may lower the amount according to ability to pay. This is a sanctuary valuation schedule; the chapter does not explain it as a measure of personal dignity.

questions.question: How does the payment table vary by age and sex?
questions.answer: For ages twenty to sixty, the stated male and female amounts are fifty and thirty shekels; for ages five to twenty, twenty and ten. From one month to five years they are five and three, and from sixty upward fifteen and ten. The law supplies the age-and-sex bands without explaining why each amount is chosen.

questions.question: Do inherited and purchased fields have the same outcome at Jubilee?
questions.answer: An inherited field that is not redeemed under the stated conditions becomes holy property belonging to the priests at Jubilee. A dedicated field bought from someone else is valued only for the years remaining and returns at Jubilee to its ancestral owner. Dedication therefore does not erase the original owner’s claim to a purchased field.

questions.question: What happens if someone exchanges a dedicated animal?
questions.answer: An animal eligible for sacrifice becomes holy when given and may not be swapped for a better or worse animal. If an exchange happens anyway, both the original and replacement become holy; an unclean animal instead receives priestly valuation and may be redeemed with an added fifth.

questions.question: What does it mean to redeem a house or field?
questions.answer: Redemption means paying the established value, usually with an added fifth, so the dedicated property remains or returns to the dedicator. Field value also declines with years remaining before Jubilee, and failure to redeem can transfer a possessed field to the priests.

questions.question: Why can a firstborn animal not be newly dedicated?
questions.answer: Verse 26 says an eligible firstborn already belongs to Yahweh as firstborn, so a person cannot create a second dedication by vow. An unclean firstborn follows a valuation-and-redemption process instead and may be sold if it is not redeemed.

questions.question: What does “permanently devoted” mean?
questions.answer: Verse 28 describes a category of person, animal, or field that cannot be sold or redeemed and is called most holy to Yahweh. The chapter distinguishes this irreversible status from ordinary dedications that may be valued and bought back.

questions.question: Who is the person “devoted to destruction” in verse 29?
questions.answer: Verse 29 says a person devoted to destruction cannot be ransomed and must be put to death. It names no particular case or procedure for imposing that status, while the preceding sections regulate ordinary vows through payment and redemption. The death clause therefore cannot be treated as saying every vow involving a person calls for human sacrifice.

questions.question: How are produce and livestock tithes handled?
questions.answer: A tenth of seed, fruit, herd, and flock is holy to Yahweh. Produce may be redeemed with an added fifth, but the tenth animal passing under the rod may not be selected by quality or exchanged; an attempted exchange makes both animals holy.

glossary.def: A priestly or fixed monetary amount attached to a vow or dedicated property, not a measure of human dignity.
To buy back something dedicated by paying its assigned amount and, where required, an added fifth.
The first offspring of an animal, treated here as already belonging to Yahweh rather than available for a new dedication.
A tenth of land produce or herd and flock animals designated as holy to Yahweh.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The preceding chapter has presented covenant blessings, severe curses, exile, confession, and remembered covenant, concluding with the laws given through Moses at Sinai. The final chapter turns to the financial and property consequences of dedications.

here.text: Valuation and redemption rules distinguish persons named in vows, animals, houses, fields, firstborn animals, devoted things, and tithes. A final formula closes Leviticus as commandments given to Moses for Israel at Sinai.

after.text: Leviticus ends at Sinai. Numbers opens with God speaking to Moses from the Tent of Meeting in the same wilderness, now ordering a census of men eligible for war; the camp’s organization becomes the next subject.
